awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I: A Platform of Biomimetic Mucins for Addressing Recurrent Infections
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project is the development of effective treatments for recurrent bacterial infections, using biomimetic mucins that restore mucosal tissue homeostasis. Native mucins are a category of molecules that defend mucosal surfaces against infection by selectively domesticating pathogenic microbial populations while supporting commensal populations. When mucosal surfaces are compromised, pathogens can overgrow and cause recurrent infections. Gum disease, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and bacterial vaginosis (BV) are all recurrent bacterial infections which affect billions of people worldwide. These seemingly unrelated ailments share the common root cause of compromised mucosal barriers. By developing biomimetic mucins, this project improves upon existing standard-of-care treatments, which address symptoms of disease but do not rectify the underlying mucosal disruption, leading to high rates of recurrence. This project aims to develop scalable and cost-effective biomimetic mucins that exhibit native-like functionalities and can be delivered to mucosal surfaces by incorporation into personal care and dietary supplements. Successful commercialization of this technology will result in a significant reduction in infection and recurrence rates, coupled with a reduction in the associated healthcare expenditures.

This Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project will create the first library of biomimetic mucins screened for microbial susceptibility mechanisms—including bacteriostatic, bactericidal, and anti-biofilm activities—against key pathogenic bacteria involved in recurrent infections. To date, biomimetic mucins development has taken an analog discovery route and requires long development timelines that impede commercialization efforts. This project introduces a multiplexed approach for producing and screening a biomimetic mucin library against a wide variety of hallmark pathogenic/commensal microbial strains and epithelial cells for streamlining the discovery route. The goals of this project are to (1) build a library of biomimetic mucins that captures relevant diversity of native mucins (2) screen the library against hallmark microbial strains typical of mucosal surfaces and (3) confirm the cytocompatibility against human epithelial cells. To accomplish these goals multiplexed tools and assays will be pioneered for chemical synthesis and bioactivity evaluation of biomimetic mucins. The output of this undertaking will be a foundational dataset of structure-activity relationships from which top-performing biomimetic mucin variants will be identified for scaled-up manufacturing, in-vivo efficacy testing, and commercialization efforts.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Kapha Bio is developing a new class of glycoproteins designed to influence microbial behavior associated with dysbiosis through a mechanism distinct from conventional antibiotics, offering a novel approach for millions of people worldwide affected by these conditions. Mucins form the main component of mucus, which lines every mucosal surface of the body, including the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, mouth, and vagina, where these molecules maintain host-microbiome homeostasis and prevent inflammation and infection. When the mucin layer is degraded, by aging, environmental exposure, medication side effects, or genetic factors, the balance of the microbiome shifts toward disease-associated bacteria, driving conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, gum disease, and bacterial vaginosis. Current treatments, largely antibiotics and over-the-counter remedies, manage symptoms without repairing the underlying mucin barrier, contributing to high rates of recurrence. Supplementing the body's own mucin with an external, mucin-like material is a promising strategy, but prior attempts to manufacture such materials at scale have failed due to low yields, complex purification, and hazardous chemistries, and naturally sourced animal-derived alternatives are inconsistent and poorly suited to commercial use.

Kapha Bio has developed a biomimetic mucin ingredient that replicates the ability of natural mucins to regulate microbial behavior and protect underlying tissue, using a scalable, safe, and reproducible synthesis process. This Small Business Technology Transfer Phase I project tested the hypothesis that these lab-made mucin mimics can be tuned to have site-specific protective properties distinct from the plain sugars or silk proteins used to make them, and addressed technical hurdles associated with systematically evaluating biomimetic mucin efficacy across a variety of therapeutic use cases. Native mucins defend the body against microbial infection of mucosal surfaces by selectively domesticating pathogenic microbial populations while supporting commensal populations, and Kapha Bio's biomimetic mucins were designed and tested to recapitulate this selective activity.

Over the course of the project, Kapha Bio expanded its biomimetic mucin library from 5 prior demonstrated variants to 20 variants spanning distinct saccharide identities, conjugation densities, and molecular weights, and developed a suite of analytical methods to confirm conjugation fidelity, purity, and molecular weight. A multiplexed screening approach was then pioneered and applied across hallmark pathogenic and commensal microbial strains representing gastrointestinal, oral, vaginal, and skin applications, as well as human epithelial cell models, to evaluate each variant's ability to prevent and disrupt bacterial biofilms, the protective structures bacteria form that make infections difficult to treat, without harming beneficial bacteria or human cells. This screening generated a Structure-Activity Relationship (SAR) analysis linking sugar identity, density, and molecular weight to microbial and cytocompatibility outcomes, confirming that biomimetic mucins possess unique, application-specific properties distinct from either the sugar or silk components alone, and that different formulations can be tailored to different applications rather than acting as a single, one-size-fits-all treatment.

This work produced a first-of-its-kind dataset connecting the molecular design of a mucin-mimic to its biological performance. One variant, since named KBB-1, emerged as the clear lead candidate: it demonstrated significant, non-antibiotic biofilm inhibitory activity against pathogens across all four target categories, and disrupted existing biofilms from gastrointestinal, oral, and vaginal pathogens, all without killing bacteria outright, an important distinction from antibiotics, which drive resistance and disrupt healthy microbial communities. KBB-1 also remained non-toxic to commensal bacteria and cytocompatible across in vitro and full-thickness mucosal tissue models, and additional testing conducted outside this award confirmed it was safe and well tolerated in a human skin study. To meet the material demands of this expanded testing, Kapha Bio transferred its benchtop synthesis process to a pilot-scale manufacturing facility, successfully producing larger batches of KBB-1 sufficient to support both Phase I testing and planned Phase II work.

Taken together, this Phase I project established the technical feasibility of Kapha Bio's biomimetic mucin platform and identified a lead candidate with broad-spectrum, non-antibiotic activity against pathogens implicated in common recurring infections affecting the gut, mouth, skin, and reproductive health. This technology offers a fundamentally different approach to managing microbiome-related disease: rather than killing bacteria, it restores the protective barrier that keeps a healthy microbiome in balance, addressing the root cause of recurrent infection, compromised mucin, rather than only its symptoms. Combined with customer discovery conducted through the NSF I-Corps program, this work positions Kapha Bio to develop a breakout category of targeted, scalable, and cost-effective specialty ingredients for personal care and dietary supplement products that consumers can access without a prescription. With continued development, this platform has the potential to significantly reduce infection and recurrence rates, which affect billions of people worldwide, lower associated healthcare expenditures, and open a new, non-antibiotic category within the broader effort to combat antimicrobial resistance.
